title: AVWAP Reclaim
teaches: The AVWAP reclaim as we trade it: a stock above its 200-day falls hard from a high everyone can see, closes under the anchored VWAP from that high for weeks until the line flattens, then closes clearly back over it; we buy only after price proves the reclaim, never at the touch, the stop sits a few cents under the reclaim day's low, a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

questions.q: On a daily chart, what does an AVWAP anchored to a stock's high show?
choices: Volume-weighted cost since the anchor
The average close of the last 50 days
The highest price since the anchor day
The open price of the anchor day
questions.why: Volume-weighted cost since the anchor. The AVWAP is the average price paid since the anchor day, weighted by volume, so busy days count more. It is not a fixed level: it moves with every day after the anchor. ChartSchool: it shows whether the bulls or bears have been in charge since a very specific time.
questions.lesson_line: The AVWAP is the average buyer's cost since one event. Name the event first.

wrong.The open price of the anchor day: The anchor day is where the sum starts. The line moves with every day after it.
wrong.The average close of the last 50 days: That is a 50-day moving average. It has no anchor and no volume weight.
wrong.The highest price since the anchor day: That is a level, not an average. The AVWAP is the average price paid, weighted by volume.

questions.simple: It shows the average price buyers have paid since the high, with busy days counting more.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, av.daily_bars (+2)
a wrong choice was shortened in the first cold check (+1)

questions.q: Back over the AVWAP from a prior high, the average buyer since that high is winning again.
questions.why: True. Shannon says the AVWAP from a prior high tells him whether the average participant since that high is winning or losing. ChartSchool says the line shows whether bulls or bears have been in charge since one specific time. Back over the line, that average buyer is winning again, and Shannon says buyers are in control. It is a place to look for evidence, not a mechanical signal.
questions.lesson_line: Under the line, the average buyer since the high is losing. Back over it, they are winning again.

A Remount of a moving average
A U&R of the prior swing low
A breakout over a flat level

Yes; it closed back over the line
No; it must close a full ATR over
Yes; a rising line makes it stronger

wrong.Yes; it closed back over the line: A close back over is not enough. Our reclaim comes after weeks of closes under a line that has flattened.

wrong.No; it must close a full ATR over: Our card wants the close 0.3 to 1.0 ATR over the line, not a full ATR. The real miss is too few closes under.

questions.q: After the buy, an AVWAP reclaim that trades down to the stop is sold at the stop.
questions.why: True. The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. Shannon: don't hold and hope.
questions.lesson_line: My stop is my stop. That is the whole rule.

questions.q: How does that grade the reclaim in your list?
questions.story: A correction just ended. Four software names reclaim their AVWAPs from their highs in the same week, yours among them.
choices: Up: the group is moving together
Down: the trade is too crowded
No change; only the chart counts
Up, but only if volume is heavy
questions.answer: Up: the group is moving together
questions.why: Up. Our card proposes several stocks in one group reclaiming together as a grade marker. It is best after a correction ends, when leaders first get back above their AVWAPs from their highs. That is this story. It is a proposed grade marker on our card, not a gate.
questions.lesson_line: One reclaim is a stock. Several in one group is a move.

wrong.No change; only the chart counts: The card makes the group a grade marker. It counts.
wrong.Down: the trade is too crowded: Our card reads a group reclaiming together as a grade marker, not as crowding.
wrong.Up, but only if volume is heavy: The marker is the group reclaiming together. Volume is not part of it.

questions.simple: Up, because several stocks in one group reclaiming together right after a correction is a plus for the grade.

reasons: cites only one fact
rests on a proposed card criterion (av.group_reclaims)

questions.q: What did the stop do?
questions.story: A 7.6 ATR fall, 47 closes under, a flat line. You bought at 262.81, stop 255.97. Day 2 takes the stop. In the weeks after, its low is 12.7% under your buy.
choices: Its job: a planned 1R loss
Cost you; it needed room
Nothing; the line was the exit
It proved the setup was bad
questions.why: Its job. Everything in the picture was right: a 7.6 ATR fall, 47 closes under, a flat line. The reclaim simply failed, and the stop said so. The stop was 2.6% under the buy and cost 1R. In the weeks after, the low was 12.7% under the buy. Holding would have cost about five times as much.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working.

wrong.Cost you; it needed room: Room meant a 12.7% hole. The stop cost 1R; holding would have cost about five times that.
wrong.Nothing; the line was the exit: The stop is the exit, not a close under the line. Here the stop did the work.
wrong.It proved the setup was bad: Everything in the picture was right. The reclaim simply failed, and a stop is for exactly that.

questions.simple: It did its job, because it kept the loss to the planned 1R while holding would have lost about five times more.

reasons: rests on held decision D-008
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: Buy again?
questions.story: You were stopped out the day after you bought. Weeks later the setup forms again and its trigger trades.
choices: Yes, as a new trade, new stop
No; one try per line, no more
Yes, but with a wider stop
No; wait a month after a stop-out
questions.answer: Yes, as a new trade, new stop
questions.why: Yes, as a new trade. Our rule: after a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again. It is a new trade with its own stop and every rule. A second rule caps it: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock. There is no waiting period. A stop-out is not a verdict on the stock.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a verdict on the level. The next trigger is a new trade.

wrong.No; one try per line, no more: The limit is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month, not one.
wrong.Yes, but with a wider stop: A new trade gets its own stop, by default a few cents under the day's low. Nothing calls for a wider one.
wrong.No; wait a month after a stop-out: No rule makes you wait. A new trigger is a new trade, within 3 tries a week and 6 a month.

questions.simple: Yes, a new trigger is a new trade with its own stop, and our rules allow up to 3 tries a week.

deeper.example: LIN, September 2019. Bought 2019-09-13 at 192.63 with a stop at 189.29, it was stopped the next session. Then it held the line for weeks, and the 3R level printed 39 sessions later without us. The stop was still right. A second buy would have needed a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B21 and E56 (+2)
two wrong choices were shortened in the first cold check (+1)

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
questions.story: Your AVWAP long closed Thursday at 2.7R. Friday it gaps open at 3.3R.
choices: Sell a third at the open
Wait for the close to decide
Sell it all at the open
Raise the stop and hold all
questions.answer: Sell a third at the open
questions.why: Sell a third at the open. Our rule: if a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. The first trim, by our hard rule, is a third at 3R. It opened at 3.3R, past 3R, so the trim is taken at the open price. The other two thirds wait for 5R and the trail.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through a trim level is the trim. Take it.

wrong.Raise the stop and hold all: The stop can rise too, but the trim is the rule at the open.
wrong.Wait for the close to decide: The level is already passed. Our rule takes the trim at the open.
wrong.Sell it all at the open: A third at 3R. Another third waits for 5R, and the last third rides the trail.

questions.simple: Sell a third at the open, because a gap past the 3R trim level fills that trim right away.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, F63 and B19 (+2)

questions.q: An AVWAP reclaim gets 20 trading days to get past 1R before it is sold.
questions.why: False. Our time stop is 10 trading days, not 20. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. The price stop still applies the whole time.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.
questions.simple: False. If it is still under 1R after 10 trading days, not 20, we sell it.

reasons: cites only one fact
rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: When does the stop move to breakeven on an AVWAP reclaim winner?
choices: Once it is up between 2R and 5R
The day after entry, to be safe
Never; the stop stays where it is
As soon as it closes over the line
questions.answer: Once it is up between 2R and 5R
questions.why: Between 2R and 5R. Our rule moves the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The stop only moves up, never down, so up to breakeven is allowed. It is a range of gain, not a fixed day.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R of gain, not on day one.

wrong.The day after entry, to be safe: Breakeven waits for 2R to 5R of gain. A day after entry is far too soon.
wrong.Never; the stop stays where it is: The stop only moves up. Up to breakeven at 2R to 5R is allowed.
wrong.As soon as it closes over the line: Every reclaim closes over the line. That is the setup, not a gain of 2R.

questions.simple: Once the trade is up between 2R and 5R, because that is when our rule moves the stop to breakeven.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, A4)
key reworded in this upgrade

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: The reclaim triggers. The reclaim day's low sits 4.1% under your fill, wider than your usual stop.
choices: Keep it; buy fewer shares
Pull the stop up to within 3%
Use the AVWAP as the stop
Same shares; the stop is honest
questions.why: Keep the stop and buy fewer shares. Our card: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. If the honest stop is wider, size down from it; if it does not fit the risk, skip. Never tighten it into the noise to make it fit. Our rulebook: stop first, and the size comes from the stop. A wider stop is not wrong. It means fewer shares.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop.

wrong.Use the AVWAP as the stop: The line is not the stop. Ours goes a few cents under the reclaim day's low.
wrong.Same shares; the stop is honest: The stop is honest, but the size comes from it. Same shares on a wider stop risks more than planned.
wrong.Pull the stop up to within 3%: That is tightening into the noise to fit the size. The card says never.

questions.simple: Keep the honest stop and buy fewer shares, or skip the trade if even that does not fit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, A3, A5 and A13 (+2)

questions.q: In our scan, reclaim days on the loudest volume reached 3R more often than quiet ones.
questions.why: False. In our scan, reclaim days on 1.5x the 50-day volume or more reached 3R 22.3% of the time. Days under 1.0x reached it 27.0% of the time. Loud volume did not help. This is what our data measured, not a rule and not a promise.
questions.lesson_line: In our scan, loud reclaim-day volume did not pick the winners.
questions.simple: False. In our data, the quiet reclaim days reached 3R a bit more often than the loud ones.

deeper.counter: It is tempting to want heavy volume on the day a stock takes back a line. Our scan of AVWAP reclaims did not back that. Days on 1.5x the 50-day average or more reached 3R 22.3% of the time. Days under 1.0x reached it 27.0%. It is one scan of our own daily bars: a measure, not a rule.

reasons: cites only one fact
a scan statistic that can change with the data
rests on held decision D-006 (volume as a cue)

questions.q: What changes on your next AVWAP reclaim?
questions.story: Bought at 43.22, stop 42.43. The next session takes the stop. The next 10 closes are all back under the line. Its low over the next twenty sessions is 11.6% under your buy.
choices: Nothing; the rules worked
Widen the stop on the next one
Stop trading AVWAP reclaims
Buy the dip under the line
questions.why: Nothing. You followed every rule and the reclaim failed. The stop took you out the next session at 1R. All of the next 10 closes were back under the line. The low over the next 20 sessions was 11.6% under the buy. The stop is the exit, so the same stop goes on the next trade.
questions.lesson_line: You will take this loss again. It is the price of the ones that run.

wrong.Buy the dip under the line: That adds to a failed reclaim. The stop is the exit, and it never moves down.
wrong.Widen the stop on the next one: A wider stop here would have ridden it down 11.6%. The stop worked.
wrong.Stop trading AVWAP reclaims: One planned loss is not a verdict on the setup. In our examples the stop kept each failure to 1R.

questions.simple: Nothing, because you followed the plan and the stop kept a small loss from becoming a much bigger one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: Take it by our card?
questions.story: Price closes back over the AVWAP from a September high. Over the 10 sessions before, that line fell 0.56 ATR.
choices: No; the line had not flattened
Yes; it closed over the line
Yes; a steep line breaks harder
No; it needs a close 1 ATR over
questions.answer: No; the line had not flattened
questions.why: No. Our card proposes a flattened line. The AVWAP fell less than 0.5 ATR over the 10 sessions before the reclaim. This one still fell 0.56 ATR, so it fails. Shannon: a move above a declining VWAP will often fail. The steeper the angle, the likelier the move fails. The close over the line is one gate; this is another.
questions.lesson_line: A move above a declining line will often fail. Wait for it to flatten.

wrong.Yes; it closed over the line: The close is one gate. The flattened line is another, and this fails it.
wrong.Yes; a steep line breaks harder: Shannon says the steeper the angle, the likelier the move across fails.
wrong.No; it needs a close 1 ATR over: Right verdict, wrong reason. The card wants 0.3 to 1.0 ATR over, not 1 ATR. The falling line fails it.

questions.simple: No, the line was still falling, and our card waits for it to go flat before a reclaim counts.

deeper.trap: AAPL, October 2021, failed this test: its line still fell 0.56 ATR in the 10 sessions before the reclaim. It reached 9.3R anyway. That does not make the rule wrong. The rule is a quality filter, not a prediction. It keeps you out of the weaker case, and some weaker cases still win.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, av.line_flattened, whose 0.5 ATR is the dossier's number (+2)

questions.q: Does it qualify as an AVWAP reclaim?
questions.story: A stock falls 3.9 ATR from a one-month high, closes under the AVWAP from that high 19 times, then closes back over.
choices: No; the fall is too small
Yes; it closed back over
Yes; 19 closes under is enough
No; it must fall 10% first
questions.answer: No; the fall is too small
questions.why: No. Our card proposes a real fall first: the anchor high minus the lowest low after it is at least 4 ATR. This dip was 3.9 ATR, so it falls short. It is a dip from a one-month high, not a real fall. The fall is measured in ATR, not in percent. The closes under the line and the close back over do not make up for it.
questions.lesson_line: Near enough is not a rule. The fall is a gate.

wrong.Yes; it closed back over: The close over is the last step. The fall behind it has to be real first.
wrong.Yes; 19 closes under is enough: Time under is one test. The fall is another, and this one fails it.
wrong.No; it must fall 10% first: Our card measures the fall in ATR, not in percent. The miss here is 3.9 ATR against 4.

questions.simple: No, it fell 3.9 ATR, short of the 4 ATR our card wants before a reclaim counts.

deeper.trap: ADC, January 2019: a 3.9 ATR dip from a one-month high, reclaimed after 19 closes under. It reached 6.4R, and the rule still rejects it by a tenth of an ATR. A winner skipped by a rule is not a mistake. The rule is a filter, and a filter will miss some winners.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, av.real_fall (+2)

questions.q: What is the read on that reclaim day?
questions.story: After weeks under a flat AVWAP, the stock opens under the line and closes 0.23 ATR over it.
choices: A poke inside the noise; pass
A clean reclaim; buy tomorrow
A U&R of the line; buy tomorrow
Too stretched; wait for a dip
questions.answer: A poke inside the noise; pass
questions.why: A poke, so pass. Our card proposes a reclaim-day close 0.3 to 1.0 ATR over the line. At 0.23 ATR the close is under that range. It is not stretched; it is the opposite. CAG in 2019 closed 0.23 ATR over its line, a marginal poke inside the noise. It chopped to 2.7R before the December gap did the real work.
questions.lesson_line: A hair over the line is still the line. Clear it.

wrong.A clean reclaim; buy tomorrow: Clean starts at 0.3 ATR over the line. This is inside the noise.
wrong.Too stretched; wait for a dip: The reverse. Stretched is past 1.0 ATR. At 0.23 the close is too small, not too far.
wrong.A U&R of the line; buy tomorrow: A U&R closes back above within 3 sessions. This one sat under the line for weeks.

questions.simple: A poke, because 0.23 ATR over the line is too small to count, so you pass.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, av.reclaim_day_close (+2)

questions.q: By our card, which setup is it?
questions.story: After weeks under the AVWAP from its high, a stock opens 0.91 ATR above the line and closes higher.
choices: A gap setup, not a reclaim
A clean reclaim from below
A U&R of the AVWAP line
A Remount of the AVWAP line
questions.answer: A gap setup, not a reclaim
questions.why: A gap setup, not an AVWAP reclaim. Our card proposes that the reclaim day not open more than 0.5 ATR over the line. This one opened 0.91 ATR over, so the line was never retaken from below in regular hours. The card judges it as a gap setup, a Kicker or a gap. Shannon reads a gap over AVWAPs as buyers back in control. That split is ours.
questions.lesson_line: Look at the open. A gap over the line is judged as a gap.

wrong.A clean reclaim from below: The reclaim is taken back from below during the day. This one gapped over.
wrong.A U&R of the AVWAP line: A U&R dips under a level and comes back. This gapped over a line it was under.
wrong.A Remount of the AVWAP line: A Remount takes back a moving average or a flat price level. This gapped over an AVWAP.

questions.simple: It is a gap setup, because it opened well above the line instead of taking it back from below.

deeper.counter: Shannon reads it differently. He wrote that a gap above a cluster of AVWAPs put buyers back in control. Our card keeps its own split. A reclaim day that opened more than 0.5 ATR over the line is judged as a gap setup. AGCO in September 2019 opened 0.91 ATR over its line and reached 3.1R, judged as a gap, not as an AVWAP reclaim.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, av.no_gap_over, where Shannon reads it differently (+2)
a wrong choice was shortened in the first cold check (+1)

questions.q: The stock trades 3,000,000 shares a day on average. Our volume ceiling on the position?
choices: 30,000 shares, 1% of daily volume
300,000 shares, 10% of daily volume
No ceiling if the stop is tight
3,000 shares, 0.1% of daily volume
questions.why: 30,000 shares. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 3,000,000 is 30,000. It is a ceiling, not a target. The risk math still sizes the trade; this ceiling only limits it.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume, and not a share more.

wrong.No ceiling if the stop is tight: The volume ceiling is its own rule. The stop sets the risk, not this ceiling.
wrong.300,000 shares, 10% of daily volume: That is 10% of the day's volume. Our ceiling is 1%.
wrong.3,000 shares, 0.1% of daily volume: That is 0.1% of daily volume. Our ceiling is 1%, which is 30,000 shares.

questions.simple: 30,000 shares, because we never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

questions.q: On our card, the index sitting above its AVWAP from its last major low grades a reclaim up.
questions.why: True. Our card's A+ list names the index above its AVWAP from the last low. The card means QQQ or SPY above its AVWAP from the most recent major low or follow-through day. It counts toward the grade.
questions.lesson_line: A plus on our card: the index above its own AVWAP from its last major low.
questions.simple: True. Our card counts it toward an A+ when the index is above its own AVWAP from its last big low.

reasons: cites only one fact
rests on a proposed card criterion (av.index_above_avwap)

questions.q: Take the reclaim?
questions.story: A clean reclaim on an $8 stock that trades about $5 million a day.
choices: No; under $10 and $20M a day
Yes; the reclaim itself is clean
Yes; at half size to be safe
No; only the dollar volume fails
questions.why: No. Our rule: trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one fails both: $8 a share and about $5 million a day. A clean line does not change that. TrendSpider adds that in thin markets the AVWAP itself can be distorted.
questions.lesson_line: A clean line in a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.Yes; the reclaim itself is clean: The line is fine and the stock is not ours. Liquidity comes before the chart.
wrong.No; only the dollar volume fails: Right verdict, misread rule. The $8 price fails too: the floor is $10 a share.
wrong.Yes; at half size to be safe: Size does not make a thin stock liquid. The rule bars the stock, not the size.

questions.simple: No, we only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B23 (+2)
two wrong choices were shortened in the first cold check (+1)

questions.q: Which setup is it?
questions.story: After an earnings gap up, a stock drifts back for a few days. It turns up just above the gap day's low. It never closed under the earnings AVWAP.
choices: Gap Support, buying the test
A reclaim after weeks under
A Remount of a moving average
A U&R of the gap day's low
questions.why: Gap Support. It buys a test that holds the gap-up day's low from above. The earnings AVWAP reclaim works from the other side of the line. It buys the first close back over from below, after weeks under it. This stock never went under, so it is not a reclaim.
questions.lesson_line: Above the line and holding is Gap Support. Back over it from below is the reclaim.

wrong.A reclaim after weeks under: A reclaim comes from below after weeks under the line. This never went under.
wrong.A U&R of the gap day's low: A U&R dips under a prior low and closes back above it. This one held the low and never dipped under.
wrong.A Remount of a moving average: A Remount takes back a moving average or a flat level. This stock never lost a line to take back.

questions.simple: Gap Support, because the stock turned up above the gap day's low and never went under the line.

deeper.trap: The trap is calling any bounce near an earnings gap a reclaim. Ask which side of the line the stock is on. Gap Support buys a test that holds the gap-up day's low from above. The earnings AVWAP reclaim buys the first close back over the line from below, after weeks under it.

reasons: rests on held decision D-082 (earnings anchors)

questions.q: The typical price behind our AVWAP is the average of the day's open, high and low.
questions.why: False. Typical price is the average of the day's high, low and close. The open is not in it. ChartSchool's formula: (H+L+C)/3. Our card builds the AVWAP from it: typical price times volume, summed from the anchor day, divided by the summed volume.
questions.lesson_line: High, low and close, averaged, weighted by volume, summed from the anchor.
questions.simple: False, typical price uses the high, low and close, not the open.

reasons: stable: ChartSchool's formula, re-checked 2026-11-12, and the card agree

questions.q: Brian Shannon calls a breakout above the AVWAP a mechanical signal to buy.
questions.why: False. Shannon calls the AVWAP a place to look for evidence, not a mechanical signal. TrendSpider, a charting vendor, writes that a trader may look for a breakout above it as a signal to go long. On this point we side with Shannon. The line shows where to look; the proof decides.
questions.lesson_line: The line is where to look for evidence, not what to do.
questions.simple: False, Shannon says the line is a place to look for proof, not a signal to buy.

deeper.counter: TrendSpider's help page: a trader may look for a breakout above the Anchored VWAP as a signal to enter a long position. Shannon calls the AVWAP a place to look for evidence, not a mechanical signal. On this point we side with Shannon. A cross shows where to look. A clear close back over a flattened line is the evidence.

reasons: reworded by the first cold check (+1); both quotes re-checked 2026-11-12

questions.q: Take it?
questions.story: In the last month the stock closed over its AVWAP, back under, over again and under again. Today it closes 0.5 ATR over.
choices: Pass; chop, too many crossings
Buy; it closed clearly over it
Buy; the line is well tested
Pass; a reclaim must gap over it
questions.why: Pass. Our card proposes a first reclaim, not chop: at most 2 crossings of the line in the 30 sessions before. This stock crossed it four times in a month before today. Shannon: when prices oscillate above and below the AVWAP, it indicates indecision. A clear close today does not undo the chop before it.
questions.lesson_line: Many crossings mean nobody is in control. Wait for the first clean one.

wrong.Buy; it closed clearly over it: Clearly over for the third time in a month is a poke in a chop.
wrong.Buy; the line is well tested: Crossings back and forth are indecision, not a tested ceiling.
wrong.Pass; a reclaim must gap over it: The reverse. Our card judges a gap over the line as a gap setup. The reason to pass is the chop.

questions.simple: Pass, because it crossed the line back and forth too often, which is chop, not a first clean reclaim.

deeper.trap: The trap is the word clearly. A 0.5 ATR close sits inside our card's 0.3 to 1.0 band, so the close alone looks fine. The pass comes from the history: the line has been crossed back and forth, which Shannon reads as indecision. Check the 30 sessions before the reclaim before you judge the close.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, av.first_reclaim (+2)
a wrong choice was shortened in the first cold check (+1)

questions.q: What did the scan not see?
questions.story: A 9.6 ATR fall, then a reclaim close 0.78 ATR over the line on 1.54x volume. It is stopped with 0.0R. The broad market fell that year.
choices: The market falling under it
Too little volume
A gap over the line
questions.why: The market. A clean-looking reclaim in a year the broad market fell, stopped with 0.0R. The index's own standing matters.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the line.

wrong.Too little volume: Volume was heavy, 1.54x. It did not help.
wrong.A gap over the line: Nothing in the story gapped. The miss was the market.

questions.q: What protects the last third?
questions.story: Your reclaim reached 5R and you took both trims. Then the market breaks hard and the stock starts to slide.
choices: The 10-day or 21-day trail
The original stop under the low
A close back under the AVWAP
The 50-day, sold on a touch
questions.why: The trail. Our plan takes a third at 3R and another at 5R, then trails the last third. The default trail is the 10-day average for fast movers or the 21-day for steadier ones. It sells on a close below that average. Our rule moves the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally, so the first stop is not the exit here.
questions.lesson_line: Two thirds banked; a trail decides the rest.

wrong.The original stop under the low: Our rule moves the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The last third rides the trail, not the first stop.
wrong.A close back under the AVWAP: After the buy, a close under the AVWAP is not an exit by itself. The trail decides the last third.
wrong.The 50-day, sold on a touch: Our default trail is the 10-day or the 21-day. And it sells on a close below, not a touch.

questions.simple: The 10-day or 21-day trail, because the last third is sold on a close below that average.

deeper.example: Our card keeps O, January 2020, as the chart for this lesson: it reached 5R, then fell by half. Two thirds banked at 3R and 5R are safe whatever comes next. Only the last third still rides, and a close below the trailing average ends it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51, E52)
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: Bought at 52.67, stop 51.99. You sell a third at 56.07. How many R did that third bank?
questions.why: 5R. One R is the fill minus the stop, 52.67 minus 51.99. The gain is 56.07 minus 52.67. Divide the gain by one R to get 5R. That is the second trim: a third at 3R, another third at 5R, then trail the last third. EPC reached 3R in six sessions and ran to 18.9R.
questions.lesson_line: Count every exit in R. The second third is 5R.
questions.simple: 5R, because the gain on that third is five times the gap between the fill and the stop.

deeper.trap: A common slip divides the gain by the fill price. That gives a percent gain, not an R count. Our trims are counted in R: the gain divided by the fill minus the stop.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (E51)
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: How does that grade the reclaim?
questions.story: After a deep fall, the AVWAP from the high flattens. The 50-day SMA runs flat right along it. Then the stock closes back over both.
choices: Up; the line sits at a second level
Down; too many lines in one place
No change; the 50-day is not part of it
Down; the 50-day sits overhead
questions.answer: Up; the line sits at a second level
questions.why: Up. Our card proposes an A+ cue: the AVWAP sits at a second level. That can be the 50-day SMA, a prior breakout level or another AVWAP. Here the 50-day runs right along the line. Shannon: a level is more likely to matter with confluence. ChartSchool says converging AVWAP lines can mark an especially strong area. A cue is a hint; grading stays a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: One line is a level. Two lines in one place is a shelf.

wrong.Down; too many lines in one place: Shannon: a level is more likely to matter with confluence. Our card grades a second level up.
wrong.No change; the 50-day is not part of it: The card names the 50-day as the second level that grades it up.
wrong.Down; the 50-day sits overhead: It runs along the line, not above it. A second level at the line is the card's A+ cue.

questions.q: Take it?
questions.story: A clean reclaim from a high triggers. The company's earnings reaction day is two sessions away.
choices: No; earnings are too close
Yes; the reclaim is clean
Yes; at half size for the report
No; hold rules bar it until 5R
questions.why: No. Our rule: no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. This buy would come two sessions before the reaction day, inside that window. The 5R part of the rule is about holding an open trade through a report, not a new buy. CDW in 2019 ran 22.4R from this spot, and it is still a pass.
questions.lesson_line: A winner the rules forbid is still a pass. Next time it may be a gap down.

wrong.Yes; the reclaim is clean: Clean is the chart. The calendar still says no.
wrong.No; hold rules bar it until 5R: Right verdict, mixed-up rule. The 5R test is for holding an open trade through a report, not a new buy.
wrong.Yes; at half size for the report: Size does not fix a report risk. The rule bars the new buy.

questions.simple: No, the report is two sessions away, and we take no new buy in the 3 days before a report.

deeper.trap: CDW, February 2019: a clean reclaim that ran 22.4R. The buy came two sessions before its earnings reaction day, so our rule forbids it. A winner the rule stops you from taking still teaches the rule. The next report could just as well be a gap down through your stop.

questions.q: In our scan, reclaims with stops over 3% reached 3R more often than tighter ones.
questions.why: False. In our scan, stops over 3% reached 3R 22.5% of the time. Stops of 2% to 3% did so 29.3% of the time, and stops of 2% or less 26.5%. So the widest stops reached 3R least often. This is what our data measured, not a promise. It backs our rule: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.
questions.lesson_line: A tight, honest stop is part of the edge, not just the risk.
questions.simple: False, in our scan the reclaims with stops over 3% reached 3R least often.

deeper.trap: Do not read this as proof that tight stops win. A 3R target sits three times the stop distance away, so a wider stop also puts 3R further off. The scan measured what happened, not why. Either way it backs A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

questions.q: Take it?
questions.story: The market reading is Orange. A reclaim triggers, and you grade the setup a B.
choices: No; Orange is A+ setups only
Yes; at full size as in Green
Yes; Orange means half size
No; Orange means no new longs
questions.answer: No; Orange is A+ setups only
questions.why: No. Our rulebook reads the market as a guide. Green is full risk per grade, and Yellow is smaller and fewer. Orange takes only A+ setups. Red is mostly cash and shorts. A B setup waits in Orange. Orange narrows the setups; it is not a size setting.

wrong.Yes; at full size as in Green: Full risk per grade is Green. Orange takes only A+ setups.
wrong.No; Orange means no new longs: Right verdict, wrong reading. Red is mostly cash and shorts. Orange still takes A+ setups.

questions.simple: No, in an Orange market we take only A+ setups, and this one is a B.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading Orange as half size. Orange narrows which setups you take. Yellow is the reading for smaller and fewer. A B setup waits for a better market or a better setup.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, F65 (+2)

questions.q: An A+ AVWAP reclaim in a Green market. The risk on the trade?
choices: 1% to 1.5% of the account
0.25% to 0.5% of the account
2% to 3% of the account
Whatever fits the stop
questions.why: 1% to 1.5% of the account. Our rulebook sets risk by grade: A+ 1% to 1.5%; A and B 0.5% to 1%; B- or lower 0.25% to 0.5%. In a Green market the guide is full risk per grade. The stop does not set the risk. It turns the risk into shares. One exception: a new trader starts at 0.25% until 50 journaled trades follow the rules.
questions.lesson_line: The grade sets the risk. The stop turns it into shares.

wrong.0.25% to 0.5% of the account: That is the B- or lower size. A+ is sized up.
wrong.Whatever fits the stop: The stop sets the shares, not the risk. The grade sets the risk.
wrong.2% to 3% of the account: Past every grade. A+ tops out at 1.5%, the most any grade uses.

questions.simple: Risk 1% to 1.5% of the account, because that is our risk band for an A+ setup.

deeper.trap: Whatever fits the stop is the trap. The stop sets the shares, not the risk. Pick the risk from the grade first. Then shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped. A new trader starts at 0.25% until 50 journaled trades follow the rules.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, E49, F65 and C37 (+2)

questions.q: When price reclaims the AVWAP from a high, the average holder since that high is back to even.
questions.why: True. Shannon: when they move back into a winning position, buyers are in control. Name the anchor; a line from a low tells another story.
questions.lesson_line: Every AVWAP tells one group's story. Say which group.

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first trim.
questions.story: A stock sits above a rising 200-day. After weeks under a flat AVWAP, it closes 0.5 ATR over it. The day's high is 36.40 and its low 35.80. Next session it trades over that high, at 36.41.
choices: Market 36.41; stop 35.77; third at 3R
Market 36.41; stop 35.77; all out at 3R
Market at the close; stop at the line
Market 36.41; stop 35.80; third at 3R
questions.why: Market at 36.41, stop at 35.77, a third at 3R. Entries are market orders, so the trade over the reclaim day's high is the fill. The stop sits a few cents under the reclaim day's low of 35.80, not exactly on it. The hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, trim, trail. Write it before the open.

wrong.Market at the close; stop at the line: The line is not the stop. Ours sits a few cents under the reclaim day's low.
wrong.Market 36.41; stop 35.77; all out at 3R: At 3R the hard rule takes a third, not all. Another third goes at 5R, then the rest trails.
wrong.Market 36.41; stop 35.80; third at 3R: 35.80 is the low itself. The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.

questions.simple: Buy at market at 36.41, put the stop just under the 35.80 low at 35.77, and sell a third at 3R.

deeper.trap: The near-miss is a stop right on the low at 35.80. Our rule puts it a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it, so it goes at 35.77. The other trap is selling it all at 3R. The hard rule takes a third there, another third at 5R, and trails the rest.

reasons: rests on held decisions D-003 (trigger) and D-008 (stop)

questions.q: How many reclaims do you take this week?
questions.story: A correction ended and the reading just turned Green. Seven leaders on your list are reclaiming their AVWAPs from their highs.
choices: A few; add more names as they work
All seven; Green means full risk
None; wait a month after the turn
Seven at half size; same total risk
questions.answer: A few; add more names as they work
questions.why: A few, then add more names as they work. Our rule: after a market correction, when the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions. Add more only as the first ones work. Leaders reclaiming their AVWAPs after a correction is the card's best condition. But the rule counts positions, so half size on all seven still breaks it.
questions.lesson_line: Green after a correction: a few first. Let the winners earn the next ones.

wrong.All seven; Green means full risk: Green is full risk per grade. After a correction, our rule still starts with a few positions.
wrong.None; wait a month after the turn: No rule makes you wait. Our rule starts with a few positions once the reading turns Green.
wrong.Seven at half size; same total risk: Our rule counts positions, not risk. Start with a few and add as they work.

questions.simple: Take a few first, because after a correction we add more names only once the first ones work.

deeper.trap: The trap is the half-size answer. Seven positions at half size is still seven positions. Our rule counts the number of positions: start with a few, and add more only as the first ones work. Many leaders reclaiming at once is a good sign for the market, not an order to buy them all.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, F68 (+2)

questions.q: Does the 200-day rule keep you out?
questions.story: During the fall, the October low undercut the 200-day. Now, weeks later, the reclaim day closes over the AVWAP and above the 200-day.
choices: No; the rule reads the close today
Yes; it traded under the 200-day
Yes; it must never touch the 200-day
No; a rising 200-day overrides it
questions.answer: No; the rule reads the close today
questions.why: No. Our rule: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average. Our card reads it on the reclaim day's close. An undercut weeks earlier, during the fall, does not decide it. Today's close above the 200-day does. A rising 200-day would be the better grade, but it is not what the gate reads.
questions.lesson_line: Read the rule as written: the close on the reclaim day.

wrong.Yes; it traded under the 200-day: The rule is about the close on the reclaim day, not every low before it.
wrong.Yes; it must never touch the 200-day: Touching it in the fall is history. The gate is today's close.
wrong.No; a rising 200-day overrides it: Right verdict, wrong reason. A rising 200-day is a grade cue. The gate is today's close above it.

questions.simple: No, the rule checks the close on the reclaim day, and that close is above the 200-day.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the rule as a history test. During the fall the low undercut the 200-day, and that feels like a broken stock. The gate reads one thing: the close on the reclaim day against the 200-day SMA. Above it, the gate passes. A rising 200-day is then the better grade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B26, as the card reads it (+2)

questions.q: What do you tell yourself about the volume?
questions.story: Two reclaims trigger the same day. One came on 2.5x volume, the other on 0.6x. Both pass every gate on the card.
